statement: The train-control system shall keep the train moving safely and consistently when available trackside and radio support changes from line to line.
The onboard system shall supervise both train movements and shunting movements.
The onboard system shall show the driver relevant movement and train information.
The onboard system shall intervene if movement would become unsafe or unauthorized.
The onboard system shall manage transitions between operating levels smoothly.
The driver shall acknowledge any warning or request to proceed that is tied to a movement authority or a safety-critical change.
The system shall request driver confirmation only when the situation requires driver awareness or a deliberate action.
If the driver does not respond within the allowed time, the system shall assume no confirmation and apply the predefined safe braking or protection action rather than continuing.
The system shall define a clear split of responsibilities between the onboard system and national functions.
The onboard system and national functions shall exchange the minimum necessary operational data.
The interview scope includes clarification of onboard train-control behavior.
The interview scope includes clarification of safety supervision.
The interview scope includes clarification of movement authority.
The interview scope includes clarification of transitions between operating levels.
The interview scope includes clarification of how the system interacts with existing national systems.
The onboard system shall support drivers in practice.
The onboard system shall support train movements in practice.
The onboard system shall support safe interaction with trackside and radio-based control.
The onboard train-control process varies by country and line.
Operating-level transitions are handled with local procedures.
Operating-level transitions require a fair amount of driver awareness.
A common system is needed.
The onboard system shall reduce dependence on local differences so drivers receive a consistent experience across networks.
The onboard system shall actively supervise movement.
The onboard system shall warn or intervene when needed.
The system shall reduce reliance on manual interpretation of signals and instructions.
The system shall support smoother transitions between operating levels.
The system shall provide better support when national train-control functions take over.
The system shall prevent any movement that is not authorized.
Driver confirmations for important actions shall be clear and unambiguous.
The system shall be designed so that the driver always knows the train's current state and the next expected action.
The system shall work reliably for both normal running and shunting movements.
The system shall support safety supervision and intervention as the highest-priority function.
The system shall continuously monitor the train against the permitted movement authority and the current operating conditions.
For normal running, the system shall warn the driver early and apply braking if speed, distance, or authority limits are exceeded.
For shunting, the system shall supervise movement using rules appropriate to that mode.
The system shall provide a first-stage clear warning to the driver when the situation is getting close to the limit.
The exact thresholds and timing shall be defined carefully.
Thresholds and timing may differ by operating mode and national rules.
Trains must be able to run safely across different national rail networks.
The system shall let a driver operate the train with consistent onboard supervision when trackside equipment, radio support, or operating rules change from one line to another.
The system shall reduce the risk of unauthorized movement.
The system shall help manage transitions between operating levels without putting extra burden on the driver.
The system shall support interoperability so rail operators can run cross-border services without fitting each country's control system separately.
The system shall reduce the cost of maintaining multiple onboard solutions.
The common train control system shall reduce safety incidents related to signal violations, overspeed, and movement authority errors.
The common train control system shall improve cross-border service efficiency by reducing delays at transitions and reducing operational restrictions caused by incompatible systems.
The common train control system shall reduce onboard equipment variation and lower maintenance and training costs.
The primary users of the system are train drivers.
Train drivers interact with the onboard display during operation.
Dispatchers are important stakeholders.
Dispatchers define movement authorities.
Dispatchers define operating conditions.
Rolling stock maintainers are affected by the technical requirements.
Regulators matter as stakeholders.
Regulators set the compliance expectations.
Regulators approve how the system is used across different networks.
In normal operation, the infrastructure manager or traffic control side shall establish the movement authority and any route or speed restrictions.
The movement authority and any route or speed restrictions shall be passed to the onboard system.
The driver shall follow the indications and confirm actions where required.
The system shall supervise speed and authority limits and intervene if the train would exceed them.
If conditions change, coordination shall happen through the radio or trackside interfaces.
The driver and control center shall work together to keep the movement safe.
The main project roles shall include drivers and train operators, infrastructure managers and dispatching/control centers, national safety authorities, and equipment suppliers and maintainers.

The system shall align onboard and trackside functions to common rules to support interoperability across national networks without requiring the driver to change the basic operating logic when moving from one national network to another.
The control centers shall provide valid movement authorities.
The onboard system shall continuously supervise the train against the movement authority limits.
The implementation shall be certified and consistent.
The system shall provide precise definitions for the term "movement authority."
The system shall provide precise definitions for the term "supervision."
The system shall provide precise definitions for the term "operating level."
The system shall provide precise definitions for the term "shunting."
The system shall provide precise definitions for national train-control functions.
The system shall ensure that shared terminology is used consistently because differences in terminology can cause misunderstandings between railways.
Cross-border rail operations are usually handled by fitting trains with multiple national systems or by relying on transitional arrangements and special operating procedures.
Drivers may have to switch between onboard modes.
Operations and maintenance are often organized around national systems.
The system shall enforce the core safety rule that a train must not exceed its permitted movement authority or the allowed speed for its current situation.
The system shall only allow movement when the proper authority is in place.
The system shall comply with European interoperability regulations and rail safety regulations.
The system shall create data on the trackside or radio-based control side and deliver it to the onboard system when the train enters a controlled area or when conditions change.
The infrastructure or radio control side shall generate authority and supervision information from the current traffic situation and route setting.
The onboard side shall cope with larger volumes of authority and supervision data without weakening safety or creating country-specific exceptions.
The system design shall be modular.
The system shall handle data conservatively by processing only current and relevant data.
The system shall define fallback behavior clearly.
The system shall respond fast enough for supervision and braking decisions to occur before the train reaches an unsafe state.
The system shall exhibit deterministic behavior under load.
The driver interface shall be clear, consistent, and easy to interpret under operational pressure regardless of the driver’s experience level.
The system shall provide unambiguous warnings.
The system shall provide controls that can be operated reliably in a cab environment, including by drivers who may have limited time to react.
The system shall support clearer prioritization of alarms.
For a driver who needs extra time, the system shall present information earlier and in a way that is easier to understand so the driver can respond within the required window.
The system shall support alternative ways of receiving critical information, such as audio plus visual presentation, subject to what is permitted in the certified cab configuration.
The ETCS shall only collect and transmit data that is necessary for operations, diagnostics, and compliance.
If personal or driver-linked data is involved, the data shall be protected in transmission.
Privacy rules are driven more by operator policy, national law, and the connected backend systems than by the onboard supervision function itself.
Concrete privacy safeguards should come from the system architecture, encryption, access control, and the operator’s data governance rules.
The implementation shall prove that it behaves correctly in all certified operating modes.
The implementation shall never lose the ability to supervise speed and movement authority under expected failures.
Acceptance testing shall use end-to-end testing against the approved ETCS level, national rules, and the specific onboard equipment configuration.
Validation shall combine simulation, lab integration, and controlled field trials.
Validation shall provide traceable evidence for timing, braking behavior, and fallback cases.
Validation evidence shall demonstrate to regulators that safety and performance remain stable as the system evolves.
The onboard ETCS system shall not dynamically change its safety-critical behavior based on an individual driver’s ability or experience.
The ETCS interface shall use standardized symbology and wording so that both new and experienced drivers can work with it.
The onboard architecture shall separate safety-critical functions from logging, diagnostics, and connected services so that a compromise in one area does not expose the core train-control function.
Access to data shall be tightly controlled.
The system shall provide authenticated interfaces for data access.
The system shall retain data in local storage only for the minimum necessary retention period.
Operators shall have clear rules defining who can retrieve data, for what purpose, and how retrieval is audited.
The system shall support train operations across borders or between networks that use different trackside systems.
The system shall support mixed operations including mainline running, shunting, and transitions between lines with different levels of support.
The onboard capability shall enable the train to move safely and efficiently under one onboard capability.
The system shall present the driver with the right information for the current operating level.
The system shall prevent unauthorized movement when required.
The system shall automatically apply braking intervention if the driver does not respond appropriately.
The onboard train-control capability shall interpret the movement authority and operating rules for the current line.
The system shall make the current movement authority or permitted movement limits available onboard.
The system shall make the train’s speed and position available onboard to the extent that the onboard system can determine them.
The system shall make relevant route or line-specific restrictions available onboard.
The system shall make warning status information available onboard.
The system shall make the status of braking intervention, including whether it is armed or active, available onboard.
For day-to-day driver operation, the system shall present the permitted speed.
For day-to-day driver operation, the system shall present the distance or limit ahead.
For day-to-day driver operation, the system shall present warning or confirmation prompts that require an immediate response.
The onboard system shall prioritize safety above all other concerns.
The onboard system shall maintain consistent behavior across different lines.
The system shall accept more complex or less convenient behavior when necessary to keep the train safe or to make it work reliably across multiple networks.
The system shall prioritize safety and interoperability over simplicity when there is a conflict.
In normal operation, the onboard system shall work with the infrastructure authority’s movement authority and any line-specific rules.
In unusual situations such as degraded operation, route changes, or emergencies, the onboard system shall support instructions or overrides from traffic control or the relevant national function.
The onboard system shall keep responsibility clear between the onboard system and the external control side.
The system shall ensure that states and terms are clearly distinguished so that the driver and the control side are referring to the same situation.
In normal operation, the driver shall follow the displayed movement authority.
In normal operation, the driver shall watch the speed and supervision limits.
If the system indicates a change of mode or operating level, the driver shall confirm or carry out the required transition.
If the system indicates a change of mode or operating level, the driver shall keep the train within the allowed limits.
In special situations such as shunting or degraded operation, the driver shall monitor the onboard indications closely.
In special situations such as shunting or degraded operation, the driver shall follow any extra restrictions or instructions that apply.
If the system asks for a confirmation or if braking intervention occurs, the driver shall not assume the system will resolve it on its own.
The driver should normally follow the onboard instructions unless a specific local rule or an instruction from traffic control or the national authority changes what is allowed.
If the operating condition changes, such as when the system drops to a degraded mode, the driver shall switch to the procedure that applies to that mode rather than continuing as before.
Any external authority or local restriction must be clear and recorded or communicated in the proper way.
Any external authority or local restriction must not conflict with the safety supervision already in place.
If there is a conflict or doubt, the safer restriction prevails and the driver should not improvise.
The system shall provide the driver with a very clear indication of the current supervision state.
The system shall provide the driver with any restriction or warning that affects whether the train may proceed.
If the train is in an override or release condition, the system shall show that condition unmistakably.
If the train is in an override or release condition, the system shall indicate that normal protection is reduced or suspended and that extra caution or extra rules apply.
Movement shall be permitted only when the onboard system has a valid authority or a defined release condition for the current state.
The system shall default to preventing movement whenever the state or authority is not clearly established.
For supervision or enforcement, the system shall apply a brake action strong enough to stop the train safely before the limit is exceeded.
In the most serious cases, the system shall perform a full intervention rather than just issuing a warning.
The system may use fallback behavior if the preferred brake command is not available or if the train is already in a special operating mode.
The system shall ensure a safe stop or a safe reduction of speed as the guiding rule when fallback behavior is used.
If different brake actions are defined, they shall be defined clearly so that the driver and the control side know what to expect.
If a conflict cannot be resolved clearly, the driver shall treat it as a restriction and shall not proceed beyond what is safely authorized.
If a sensor or data source fails, the system shall move to the safest workable supervision state it can maintain.
The system shall not continue operating as if a sensor or data source failure had not occurred.
If missing information affects movement authority, the system shall treat the failure as safety-relevant.
If missing information affects speed supervision, the system shall treat the failure as safety-relevant.
If missing information affects braking enforcement, the system shall treat the failure as safety-relevant.
The driver shall receive a clear fault or degraded-status indication showing what capability is lost and what limitation now applies.
If the system reduces functionality, the driver shall be informed immediately whether normal running, shunting, or further movement is still permitted.
The system shall base the fail-safe operating decision on whether the remaining onboard information is sufficient to prove safe movement authority and speed supervision.
If the remaining onboard information is sufficient, the system shall remain in a reduced supervision state.
If the remaining onboard information is not sufficient, the system shall limit movement to the safest allowed condition.
If the safest allowed condition cannot be guaranteed, the system shall enforce a stop.
The system shall show the driver the exact operating limitation in plain terms.
The driver display shall indicate when no further movement is permitted except for securing the train.
The displayed limit shall be obvious as the current authority, not merely a warning, so that the driver does not misread the condition.

Shunting or other low-speed movement shall be allowed only if the system can continue to supervise the move within a defined safe limit and the relevant local operating rules permit it in the degraded condition.
The system may change the label slightly by context if a line or national system needs a familiar term.
Drivers shall receive formal training on the meaning of the cab messages.
Drivers shall receive familiarization before operating on a new line or with a different national overlay.
The confirmation time should be long enough for a driver to read and understand the message, but short enough that safety is not left waiting.
The confirmation time should vary by message type and operating context.
Urgent safety actions should allow less confirmation time than informational prompts.
If confirmation does not arrive in time, the system should assume the driver has not accepted the command or warning and move to the safest applicable state.
If confirmation does not arrive in time, the system should cancel the pending action.
If confirmation does not arrive in time, the system should alert the driver that the request timed out.
The confirmation timeout should be shorter for urgent safety-related messages where delay could increase risk.
The onboard system shall not blindly restore the previous state and carry on after recovery.
Before the train continues in service, the system shall verify that the recovered onboard data and current operating situation are still valid.
If anything is uncertain during recovery, the system shall hold the train in the safest applicable fallback state.
The driver shall follow the prescribed recovery or local operating procedure.
If recovery depends on external authorization or trackside confirmation, that authorization or confirmation shall be received before normal service can resume.
The system shall clear the fallback state only when both the active mode and movement authority are unambiguous.
The system shall be maintained to support safety.
The system shall be maintained to support regulatory changes.
The system shall preserve interoperability across different rail networks and national overlays.
Changes to the system shall not disrupt service more than necessary.
The system shall continue working through rolling stock changes.
The system shall remain backward compatible.
If a line or authority changes its local procedures, the onboard behavior and displayed information shall evolve in a controlled way.
Any maintenance-related change shall be introduced only after it has been validated against the safety requirements and the applicable interoperability rules.
If a change affects behavior in service, it shall be staged so the train can keep operating safely.
If an update does not complete cleanly, rollback shall be available.
Service disruption shall be minimized by allowing changes during planned windows or while the train is in a safe state.
A safe-state change window requires the train to be in a stationary or otherwise protected condition.
Changes that affect core supervision must be deferred until a planned maintenance stop unless the operator has a formally approved procedure for in-service update.
Cab messages shall be short.
Cab messages shall use a fixed set of terms so that the driver sees the same meaning across different trains and lines.
Where a country requires specific wording, the system shall use that wording exactly as approved.
If messages have to be shown in a national language, the system shall use the locally mandated language for the operational content.
Fallback to a common language shall be used only where the rules permit it.
Cab messages shall support safe driving decisions quickly.
The system shall avoid free text unless it is strictly controlled and approved.
The fallback common language shall only be used when the approved local wording is missing, cannot be rendered correctly, or the operating rules explicitly allow it.
The system shall determine which version to present based on the active national and route configuration already loaded for the journey.
If there is any mismatch or uncertainty, the system shall not guess.
